statement: In two placebo-controlled trials from one San Francisco team, in men who have sex with men without current major depression (mean baseline CES-D depression scores about 17 and 20) with methamphetamine dependence who all received weekly counselling (60 men treated for 12 weeks; 120 cisgender men and transgender women treated for 24 weeks and followed 12 weeks after stopping), mirtazapine lowered the modelled weekly probability of a methamphetamine-positive urine compared with placebo: relative risk 0.57 (95% CI 0.35–0.93) at 12 weeks in the first trial and 0.67 (0.51–0.87) at 12 weeks in the second, with net relative risks of 0.75 (0.56–1.00) at 24 weeks and 0.73 (0.57–0.96) 12 weeks after medication stopped. Most urine samples stayed positive in both arms (66% vs 78% of samples provided at week 12 of the second trial), end-of-treatment abstinence did not differ significantly (18% vs 8%; OR 2.50, 0.80–7.61), adherence measured by electronic pill containers was below 50% in both arms, and drowsiness was more common on mirtazapine. The two trials share investigators, site, population and analysis model, so they are not independent replications. These trials treated methamphetamine dependence over months; the short trials of mirtazapine for the withdrawal period itself, reported in the claim on medicines for withdrawal, are different trials: pooled, they showed no difference from placebo in discontinuation, and one of them reported lower withdrawal scores, a result the review could not pool.
plain: Two small trials by the same San Francisco team, in gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (and a few transgender women) who were also getting weekly counselling, found that the antidepressant mirtazapine may lower the chance of a meth-positive urine test by roughly a quarter to two-fifths compared with a placebo. Most tests were still positive in both groups, the share of people who stopped using did not clearly differ, and drowsiness was more common on the medicine. No independent team has repeated it, and it has not been tested in other groups of people. Two other, short trials of mirtazapine for withdrawal symptoms are a separate question, described elsewhere in this section.
population: Cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men, without current major depression, with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence and a methamphetamine-positive urine at entry, receiving weekly counselling (San Francisco)
exposure: Mirtazapine daily for 12 weeks (first trial) or 24 weeks (second trial)
comparator: Matched placebo with the same weekly counselling
outcome: Methamphetamine-positive weekly urine (qualitative test); end-of-treatment urine-defined abstinence
magnitude: First trial (n=60): RR 0.57 (0.35–0.93) at 12 weeks; raw final-visit positivity 44% vs 63% (editors' RR 0.71, 0.42–1.18). Second trial (n=120): RR 0.67 (0.51–0.87) at 12 weeks; net RR 0.75 (0.56–1.00) at 24 weeks and 0.73 (0.57–0.96) at 36 weeks; raw positivity 66% vs 78%, 63% vs 74% and 71% vs 88%; end-of-treatment abstinence 18% vs 8% (OR 2.50, 0.80–7.61). Editors' crude week-12 risk ratio in the second trial, from the samples provided (25 of 38 vs 32 of 41): 0.84 (0.64–1.12). The modelled risk ratios measure how far the two arms' fitted trends diverged after allowing for the fitted baseline difference; the mirtazapine arm began with more positive urines (85% vs 75%), one reason the modelled ratios lie further from 1 than the crude contrasts (editors' reading).

grade.reasoning: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials (180 participants). Risk of bias: in the first trial the registered primary outcome was changed from feasibility to efficacy during recruitment; in the second, 34–41% of urine results were missing at each assessment, with more dropout on mirtazapine, and the analysis assumes data missing completely at random. Indirectness: only sexual-minority men without current major depression and five transgender women, all receiving counselling, and the outcome is urine positivity rather than abstinence or functioning. Imprecision considered but not rated down: both trials' intervals for the primary outcome exclude no effect, although the 24-week upper limit reaches 1.00 and abstinence intervals are wide. Not counted as independent replication (METHODS §6.3). The second trial reports that the effect stayed significant when missing urine samples were counted as positive, when week-1 results were included and when baseline correlates of missingness were adjusted for, with the estimates only in a supplement the editors have not read; the analysis stratified by intensity of use showed no significant effect. A blinding check at week 24 found 46% vs 49% guessing their arm correctly (P = .83). The risk-of-bias downgrade therefore rests on the amount of missing data and the differential dropout, not on a demonstrated distortion.

evidence.extracted: The Methods describe five sensitivity analyses: including week-1 results; imputing missing urine samples as positive (a not-missing-at-random assumption); adjusting for imbalanced baseline characteristics and baseline correlates of missing or positive samples; including late final visits; and stratifying by baseline intensity of use. The text does not say whether these were prespecified; only the primary model is called prespecified. The Results report significant effects favouring mirtazapine with week-1 results included, with missing samples imputed as positive and with baseline correlates controlled for, giving the estimates only in the supplement's eTable (not read). No significant effect was seen when stratifying by intensity of use, and the late-visit analysis is not reported in the text. No evidence of unblinding at week 24: 19 (46%) on mirtazapine and 23 (49%) on placebo guessed their arm correctly (P = .83).
